extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy; economists and policymakers interested in labour, profits, and market policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying classical political-economy principles about what causes differences in wages and profits across employments and places, and how policy (corporations, apprenticeships, restrictions) modifies those inequalities. The page gives causal criteria, examples, and policy evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit affected by agreeableness and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the five circumstances that vary wages of labour, two only affect the profits of stock: the agreeableness or disagreeableness of the business, and the risk or security with which it is attended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreeable or disagreeable business conditions and the degree of risk alter ordinary profits; inland trades are generally less uncertain than foreign trade, and certain foreign routes differ in risk (e.g., North America vs Jamaica).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit rises with risk but not proportionally
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary rate of profit rises more or less with the risk, but not in proportion to it and not so as to compensate it completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-risk trades show more bankruptcies; competition among adventurers in hazardous trades can reduce profit below what would fully compensate risk (example: smuggling yields high gains when successful but high bankruptcy rate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparent profit from wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent profits in some trades often include disguised wages — remuneration for skill, trust, or labour is charged as part of the price and appears as profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: apothecaries' high mark-ups may mainly be payment for their skill/trust (physician to poor/rich), and small grocers' high percentage returns often include substantial compensation for their labour and skills; deducting reasonable labour wages reduces apparent profit to ordinary profits of stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of market influences percent vs absolute profits and accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller markets yield higher percentage profits on small capitals but lower absolute sums and reduced capacity for accumulation; larger markets allow extension of trade and greater absolute profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grocer in a small sea-port may make 40–50% on £100 stock but only small annual accumulation; a wholesale merchant on £10,000 may make 8–10% but accumulate far more. Thus great fortunes are more likely in large towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market extent affects consumer prices via prime cost and profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the market both diminishes apparent profit (by enabling larger stock and lower percentage mark-up) and can increase prime cost (by requiring supplies from farther away), which often counterbalance in final consumer prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grocery goods often cheaper in capitals due to lower mark-ups and same prime cost; bread and meat may be as cheap or dearer depending on transport distances and local prime cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative trade produces volatile, non-regular profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative merchants change the branch of trade according to expected profit, so their profits and losses bear no regular proportion to those of any one established branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculation (e.g., shifting between corn, wine, sugar, tobacco) requires extensive commerce and intelligence available only in large towns; success can produce sudden fortunes but failure equally sudden losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three requisites for equality of advantages across employments
rubrics_metrics.description: For equality in the whole advantages/disadvantages of different employments, three things are required: (1) employments must be well known and long established locally; (2) they must be in their ordinary (natural) state; (3) they must be the sole or principal employments of those who occupy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these three conditions hold, the non-pecuniary advantages/disadvantages and pecuniary returns tend to balance across employments; violation of any produces inequalities even under perfect freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: New manufactures temporarily raise wages to attract labour
rubrics_metrics.description: When establishing a new manufacture or branch, higher wages are initially required to entice workers from other employments until the trade becomes established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufactures driven by fashion/fancy change often and thus pay higher wages than manufactures demanded by necessity; example comparison: Birmingham (fashion goods) vs Sheffield (necessity goods) show wage differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand fluctuations cause wage and profit variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for different kinds of labour and commodities sometimes exceeds or falls below usual levels, causing wages and profits to rise or fall accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal demand (hay-time, harvest), wartime conscription of sailors, or decaying manufactures illustrate how temporary scarcity or surplus of labour affects wages; analogous effects occur for stock/profits with commodity price changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commodity supply variability determines price/profit stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commodities yield nearly constant annual output (e.g., linen, woollen cloth) so prices only vary with demand; others (corn, wine, sugar, tobacco) have large year-to-year quantity variation so prices — and profits for some dealers — fluctuate greatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative merchants focus on commodities with volatile supply/price; in stable-output industries producers and dealers face steadier profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation privileges and apprenticeship regulations restrict competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive privileges of corporations (including limits on number and duration of apprenticeships) restrain competition in trades and towns to fewer persons than would otherwise enter them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sheffield bye-law limiting apprentices, Norfolk & Norwich limit for master weavers, national statutes (Statute of Apprenticeship under Elizabeth) creating seven-year terms and restricting some trades to market towns; these limit entry and increase education expense to restrain competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long apprenticeships are ineffective for quality control and are socially costly
rubrics_metrics.description: Long terms of apprenticeship give no security against fraud or poor workmanship and can be counterproductive (apprentices idle, master benefits by free labour, public pays higher prices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks/stamps on goods (sterling mark on plate, stamps on linen/woollen) provide better purchaser security than statutory apprenticeship terms; long apprenticeships reduce incentives to industry and raise costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive structure matters: piece-rate journeymen vs unpaid apprentices
rubrics_metrics.description: A journeyman paid by piece is likely to be industrious because he benefits from exertion; an apprentice with no immediate interest is likely to be idle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter, paid-on-performance training would encourage diligence and cheaper education; long apprenticeships protect masters' profits and restrict competition at public cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations coordinate to limit market supply and maintain prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Town corporations and guilds enact regulations (limits on apprentices, control of admission) to prevent the market being overstocked with their own industry — effectively keeping supply low to maintain higher prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the town such regulations often balance (they buy from one another at higher prices but can sell to the country at higher prices); the net gain comes from dealings with the country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town commerce derives advantage from adding value to country produce
rubrics_metrics.description: Towns draw subsistence and materials from the country and repay value by exporting worked-up goods or by supplying imported goods augmented by wages and merchant profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The town's advantage consists in the augmentation of price through wages and profits on goods returned to the country or exported; this explains towns' roles in regional economy and how regulations within towns affect the wider economy.
